extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, humorists, and literary performers (writers, actors) seeking craft/advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical literary advice on producing and presenting humor and poetry: how inspiration relates to craft, how works mature, and how public reception affects a writer/performer's career. Includes guidance for actors about comedic vs. serious roles and stylistic observations for writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep wit in the background until you have a reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: If I were giving advice to a young fellow of talent, with two or three facets to his mind, I would tell him by all means to keep his wit in the background until after he had made a reputation by his more solid qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: build solid credentials first (serious work), then reveal comic talent. The text cites Sydney Smith and advises 'Hamlet first, and Bob Logic afterwards' as a strategy for maintaining credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the ridiculous with seriousness (laughter and tears)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sense of the ridiculous is one side of an impressible nature, it is very well; but if that is all there is in a man, he had better have been an ape... Laughter and tears are meant to turn the wheels of the same machinery of sensibility; one is wind-power, and the other water-power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on being funny; cultivate serious faculties as well so your work can also move or mean something beyond mere amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about trying to be serious after being a known humorist
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a very dangerous thing for a literary man to indulge his love for the ridiculous. People laugh with him just so long as he amuses them; but if he attempts to be serious, they must still have their laugh, and so they laugh at him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career implication: if public perception fixes you as a humorist, attempts at seriousness risk being undermined by audience expectations and derision (example of critics attacking Sydney Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic inspiration (soul) from the written copy (body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every such poem has a soul and a body, and it is the body of it, or the copy, that men read and publishers pay for. The soul of it is born in an instant in the poet’s soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative process guidance: recognize inspiration is instantaneous but the craft of producing a readable copy requires time and work; do not confuse the two when evaluating or preparing work for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge new poems in their 'green state' — allow maturation
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t think the poems I read you sometimes can be fairly appreciated, given to you as they are in the green state... A poem must be kept and used, like a meerschaum or a violin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: give poems time and use to age—repetition, performance, and readership help the parts knit together; immediate judgment of fresh work is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: A genuine poem should be porous enough to absorb readers' humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine poem is capable of absorbing an indefinite amount of the essence of our own humanity — its tenderness, its heroism, its regrets, its aspirations, so as to be gradually stained through with a divine secondary color derived from ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for quality: poems that can take on layers of meaning and emotional resonance through repeated reading/experience are superior; aim for porousness rather than impermeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and use knit the parts of a poem into organic unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting each word as a piece, there are more pieces in an average copy of verses than in a violin... let the poem be repeated aloud and murmured over... and at length the parts become knit together in such absolute solidarity that you could not change a syllable without the whole world’s crying out against you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing/evaluation guidance: expect that repetition (oral and mental) is part of forming cohesion; allow time and exposure before making radical changes or final judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize serious roles/works before comic ones (actors/writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: And so to an actor: Hamlet first, and Bob Logic afterwards... don’t think... that people will be ready to allow that you can do anything great with Macbeth’s dagger after flourishing about with Paul Pry’s umbrella.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance career advice: obtain credibility through substantial, serious roles or works before showing lighter comedic talents, to avoid being typecast or patronized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that audiences tend to feel superior to the comic performer
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you know that you feel a little superior to every man who makes you laugh... You have a pleasant sense of patronizing him, when you condescend so far as to let him turn somersets... But if all at once the performer asks the gentleman to come upon the floor... that wasn’t in the programme!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-dynamic insight: understand the patronizing tilt in audience-performer relations; this affects how humor is received and the risks when attempting intimacy or seriousness with the same audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triadic adjective grouping as an instinctive rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural tendency in many persons to run their adjectives together in triads... He was honorable, courteous, and brave; she was graceful, pleasing, and virtuous... It is, I suspect, an instinctive and involuntary effort of the mind to present a thought or image with the three dimensions that belong to every solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic observation: using adjective triads can be an unconscious technique to give an idea a sense of 'three-dimensional' completeness; recognize it as a rhetorical device rather than mere affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity and usage lend sonority and resonance to language
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t you perceive the sonorousness of these old dead Latin phrases?... every word fresh from the dictionary brings with it a certain succulence; and though I cannot expect the sheets... to get so dry as the crisp papyrus... yet you may be sure, that, while the sheets are damp, and while the lines hold their sap, you can’t fairly judge of my performances, and that, if made of the true stuff, they will ring better after a while.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation guidance: older, established phrases and language often carry greater resonance; consider historical and tonal maturity when assessing sonority and lasting merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: A creator’s immediate affection for their work is strongest while it’s 'warm'
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as they are warm from his mind, carry any of his animal heat about them, I know he loves them,—When they have had time to cool, he is more indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note for critics and creators: be mindful that authors' attachment to newly created pieces is temporary; their own perception will change as the work cools, which affects revision and reception decisions.
